validation.note: Generated structured draft records; numeric-entry and complex-format keys require clinical/editorial completion before production exam use.

items.title: A 62-year-old reports crushing substernal pressure radiating to the jaw for 25 minutes; skin is cool and ECG shows ST elevation in contiguous leads. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Activate emergency response, obtain/interpret 12-lead ECG, establish IV access, give aspirin if not contraindicated, and prepare for reperfusion.
items.rationale: Time-dependent myocardial injury requires rapid recognition and reperfusion; assess contraindications and follow ACS protocol.

items.title: A 71-year-old develops facial droop and unilateral arm weakness 40 minutes ago; bedside glucose is 108 mg/dL. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Activate stroke pathway, establish last-known-well time, check glucose, obtain urgent noncontrast head CT, and keep NPO pending swallow screen.
items.rationale: Rapid imaging distinguishes hemorrhage from ischemia; last-known-well guides reperfusion eligibility and swallowing precautions reduce aspiration.

items.title: A client with pneumonia is febrile, confused, BP 82/46 mm Hg, HR 128/min, lactate 4.2 mmol/L. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Escalate immediately, obtain cultures without delaying antibiotics, administer prescribed broad-spectrum antimicrobials and crystalloid, and reassess perfusion.
items.rationale: Hypotension and elevated lactate suggest septic shock; timely antimicrobials, fluid resuscitation, and reassessment are essential.

items.title: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, deep respirations, glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, and potassium 5.4 mEq/L. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, deep respirations, glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, and potassium 5.4 mEq/L.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Begin isotonic IV fluids, monitor potassium and ECG, initiate IV insulin per protocol after potassium assessment, and track glucose/anion gap.
items.rationale: DKA requires volume replacement and insulin; serum potassium may be elevated despite total-body depletion and can fall rapidly with treatment.

items.title: An older adult with type 2 diabetes has profound dehydration, glucose 890 mg/dL, serum osmolality 342 mOsm/kg, and minimal ketones. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:An older adult with type 2 diabetes has profound dehydration, glucose 890 mg/dL, serum osmolality 342 mOsm/kg, and minimal ketones.|response:Prioritize isotonic fluid replacement, frequent neurologic and electrolyte assessment, and insulin per protocol after initial fluids.|rationale:Severe hyperosmolality and dehydration dominate HHS; gradual correction and close monitoring reduce neurologic and circulatory complications.
items.rationale: Severe hyperosmolality and dehydration dominate HHS; gradual correction and close monitoring reduce neurologic and circulatory complications.

items.title: A client with heart failure is acutely dyspneic, has diffuse crackles, pink frothy sputum, and SpO₂ 82%. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Acute pulmonary edema|priority:Sit upright, support oxygenation/ventilation, summon emergency assistance, and prepare prescribed diuretic/vasodilator therapy.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Pulmonary edema causes acute gas-exchange failure; respiratory support and rapid escalation take priority.

items.title: A client with acute kidney injury has potassium 6.8 mEq/L and peaked T waves on ECG. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Hyperkalemia|actions:Initiate continuous ECG monitoring, escalate urgently, prepare IV calcium for membrane stabilization and potassium-shifting/removal therapies as prescribed.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: ECG changes indicate cardiac toxicity; calcium stabilizes the myocardium while other therapies lower serum potassium.

items.title: A client receiving loop diuretics has weakness, potassium 2.7 mEq/L, and flattened T waves. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client receiving loop diuretics has weakness, potassium 2.7 mEq/L, and flattened T waves.|priority:Assess rhythm, replace potassium as prescribed using a pump, verify renal function and urine output, and recheck potassium.
items.rationale: Hypokalemia increases dysrhythmia risk; IV potassium must never be given by IV push.

items.title: A postoperative client has urine output 15 mL/hr for 3 hours and creatinine rising from 0.9 to 2.1 mg/dL. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Oliguria and rising creatinine indicate impaired renal function requiring prompt evaluation of reversible causes.

items.title: A client with COPD has increased work of breathing, wheezing, and SpO₂ 86% on room air; baseline target is 88–92%. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Controlled oxygen and bronchodilation improve hypoxemia/airflow while monitoring for hypercapnia and respiratory failure.

items.title: A 19-year-old has severe wheezing, accessory muscle use, and speaks only one word at a time. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Treat as severe exacerbation: urgent escalation, inhaled short-acting bronchodilator, systemic corticosteroid, oxygen, and reassessment.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Inability to speak full sentences and accessory muscle use indicate severe airflow obstruction.

items.title: A postoperative client develops sudden pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, dyspnea, and SpO₂ 88%. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Escalate immediately, support oxygenation, assess hemodynamic stability, and prepare for diagnostic evaluation and anticoagulation if prescribed.
items.rationale: Acute dyspnea and pleuritic pain after surgery raise concern for PE; instability requires emergency response.

items.title: A chest drainage system becomes disconnected from the chest tube while the client is coughing. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Chest tube disconnection|actions:Restore a sterile water seal per facility protocol, keep the system below chest level, assess respiratory status, and notify the provider.|evaluation:Maintaining a water seal limits air entry; never clamp a chest tube routinely because tension pneumothorax may result.
items.rationale: Maintaining a water seal limits air entry; never clamp a chest tube routinely because tension pneumothorax may result.

items.title: A client after central-line insertion develops severe dyspnea, hypotension, absent breath sounds on one side, and tracheal deviation. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Call emergency response and prepare for immediate decompression; provide oxygen and support circulation.
items.rationale: Obstructive shock with unilateral absent breath sounds is a life-threatening tension pneumothorax.

items.title: A client reports hematemesis and melena; BP is 86/52 mm Hg and HR 132/min. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Assess airway and perfusion, activate urgent response, establish large-bore IV access, prepare fluids/blood products, and trend CBC/coagulation.
items.rationale: Hemodynamic instability suggests significant hemorrhage; circulation and airway protection are priorities.

items.title: A client has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase four times the upper reference limit, and persistent vomiting. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Provide prescribed IV fluids and analgesia, monitor respiratory/renal status and electrolytes, and advance nutrition as clinically tolerated.
items.rationale: Pancreatitis care emphasizes supportive treatment, hydration, pain control, and surveillance for organ dysfunction.

items.title: A client has abdominal distention, colicky pain, bilious vomiting, and absent stool/flatus. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client has abdominal distention, colicky pain, bilious vomiting, and absent stool/flatus.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Keep NPO, initiate prescribed IV fluids, monitor electrolytes and abdominal findings, and prepare for imaging/decompression.
items.rationale: Obstruction risks fluid shifts, ischemia, and perforation; avoid oral intake until evaluated.

items.title: A client with suspected perforated viscus has rigid abdomen, rebound tenderness, fever, and tachycardia. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client with suspected perforated viscus has rigid abdomen, rebound tenderness, fever, and tachycardia.|response:Escalate urgently, keep NPO, obtain IV access, prepare broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical evaluation.|rationale:Peritoneal signs may indicate perforation and sepsis requiring urgent source control.
items.rationale: Peritoneal signs may indicate perforation and sepsis requiring urgent source control.

items.title: A client with cirrhosis is newly confused with asterixis and elevated ammonia. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Cirrhosis with encephalopathy|priority:Assess airway and neurologic status, identify precipitating factors such as bleeding/infection/constipation, and administer prescribed lactulose.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Hepatic encephalopathy requires treatment of precipitants and reduction of intestinal ammonia.

items.title: A client with atrial fibrillation reports sudden severe leg pain; the foot is pale, cool, and pulseless. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Acute ischemic limb|actions:Notify vascular team immediately, keep limb at neutral position, assess neurovascular status, and prepare for anticoagulation/revascularization.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: The six Ps indicate acute arterial occlusion; rapid intervention preserves limb viability.

items.title: A client with a tibial fracture reports escalating pain despite opioids and pain with passive toe stretch. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client with a tibial fracture reports escalating pain despite opioids and pain with passive toe stretch.|priority:Notify the provider immediately, perform frequent neurovascular checks, and prepare for emergent fasciotomy evaluation.
items.rationale: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs; palpable pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome.

items.title: After trauma, a client has hypotension, bradycardia, warm dry skin, and motor weakness below the injury. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Loss of sympathetic tone can cause hypotension and bradycardia; spinal precautions prevent secondary injury.

items.title: A client with traumatic brain injury develops decreasing level of consciousness, vomiting, and unequal pupils. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Neurologic deterioration and pupillary change suggest rising ICP and possible herniation.

items.title: A hospitalized client begins generalized tonic-clonic movements while in bed. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Protect from injury, lower bed, turn to side when possible, time seizure, do not restrain or place objects in mouth, and assess airway afterward.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Safety and airway protection are priorities; nothing should be placed in the mouth during a seizure.

items.title: A client has fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Initiate droplet precautions promptly, notify provider, obtain cultures/diagnostics as ordered, and do not delay prescribed antibiotics.
items.rationale: Suspected bacterial meningitis is time critical and requires isolation and prompt antimicrobial therapy.

items.title: A client receiving chemotherapy has temperature 38.4°C and absolute neutrophil count 300 cells/mm³. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Neutropenic fever|actions:Treat as an emergency: notify provider, obtain cultures, initiate prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly, and avoid rectal procedures.|evaluation:Fever with severe neutropenia can rapidly progress to sepsis; avoid mucosal trauma and delays.
items.rationale: Fever with severe neutropenia can rapidly progress to sepsis; avoid mucosal trauma and delays.

items.title: Fifteen minutes after packed RBCs begin, a client develops chills, back pain, and fever. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Stop transfusion, keep IV open with normal saline using new tubing, assess vitals, notify provider and blood bank, and follow reaction protocol.
items.rationale: Stopping the transfusion prevents further exposure; do not restart the same unit.

items.title: Minutes after an antibiotic, a client develops wheezing, facial swelling, urticaria, and BP 78/40 mm Hg. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Give IM epinephrine promptly per emergency protocol, call for help, support airway/oxygenation, and prepare IV fluids.
items.rationale: Epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis with airway or circulatory compromise.

items.title: A postoperative client is difficult to arouse, RR 6/min, and pupils are pinpoint after IV morphine. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Support ventilation, stimulate and call for help, administer naloxone per protocol, and monitor for recurrent respiratory depression.
items.rationale: Respiratory depression is the immediate threat; naloxone may wear off before the opioid.

items.title: A client 18 hours after last alcohol use has tremors, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and visual hallucinations. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client 18 hours after last alcohol use has tremors, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and visual hallucinations.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Initiate withdrawal assessment protocol, institute seizure/fall precautions, administer prescribed benzodiazepine, and give thiamine as ordered.
items.rationale: Withdrawal can progress to seizures or delirium tremens; benzodiazepines are first-line and thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy.

items.title: A client taking warfarin reports black stools and dizziness; INR is 5.8 and BP is 94/60 mm Hg. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client taking warfarin reports black stools and dizziness; INR is 5.8 and BP is 94/60 mm Hg.|response:Hold warfarin, assess hemodynamics, notify provider urgently, obtain CBC/type and screen, and prepare reversal therapy as prescribed.|rationale:Melena with supratherapeutic INR indicates potentially serious bleeding requiring stabilization and reversal assessment.
items.rationale: Melena with supratherapeutic INR indicates potentially serious bleeding requiring stabilization and reversal assessment.

items.title: A client receiving unfractionated heparin has platelets fall from 220,000 to 88,000/mm³ on day 6. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia|priority:Stop all heparin products, notify provider, avoid platelet transfusion unless specifically indicated, and anticipate a non-heparin anticoagulant.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: A greater than 50% platelet fall in the typical time window suggests HIT, a prothrombotic immune reaction.

items.title: An older adult taking digoxin reports nausea and yellow vision; pulse is 48/min and potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Digoxin toxicity|actions:Hold dose, obtain ECG and digoxin/electrolyte levels, notify provider, and anticipate toxicity management.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Bradycardia, visual changes, and hypokalemia increase concern for digoxin toxicity.

items.title: A client with type 1 diabetes is prescribed rapid-acting insulin before meals; the meal tray is delayed. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client with type 1 diabetes is prescribed rapid-acting insulin before meals; the meal tray is delayed.|priority:Verify glucose and meal availability; coordinate administration so rapid-acting insulin is given when food is ready per order/protocol.
items.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin can cause hypoglycemia if food is delayed or unavailable.

items.title: A client receiving magnesium sulfate has RR 10/min, absent patellar reflexes, and urine output 20 mL/hr. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Respiratory depression and absent reflexes indicate magnesium toxicity; calcium gluconate is the antidote.

items.title: A client taking lithium develops vomiting, coarse tremor, ataxia, and confusion after several days of diarrhea. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Dehydration and sodium loss reduce lithium clearance and can precipitate toxicity.

items.title: During rapid vancomycin infusion, a client develops flushing and itching of face and upper torso without airway compromise. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Pause infusion, assess airway and vital signs, notify provider, and restart more slowly if prescribed after symptoms resolve.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Rate-related histamine release can cause flushing; distinguish it from anaphylaxis and follow prescribed rate adjustments.

items.title: A client taking lisinopril develops tongue swelling and hoarseness. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Stop the medication, activate emergency airway response, and prepare for airway management.
items.rationale: ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema can rapidly obstruct the airway; airway protection takes priority.

items.title: A client taking metformin is scheduled for iodinated contrast and has eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m². The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Metformin and contrast|actions:Notify the prescriber/radiology team and follow protocol to withhold metformin around contrast and reassess renal function before restarting.|evaluation:Renal impairment increases risk of metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis; follow current contrast and renal guidance.
items.rationale: Renal impairment increases risk of metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis; follow current contrast and renal guidance.

items.title: A family member asks to press the client's PCA button while the client sleeps. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Explain that only the client should activate PCA, assess sedation and respiratory status, and reinforce safety.
items.rationale: PCA by proxy increases risk of oversedation because the client cannot self-limit doses.

items.title: A nurse prepares IV potassium chloride for a client with potassium 2.8 mEq/L. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Dilute and administer via infusion pump at prescribed rate after checking renal function and urine output; never give IV push.
items.rationale: Concentrated potassium can cause fatal dysrhythmias if administered rapidly.

items.title: A client taking long-term prednisone reports fever and has fasting glucose 220 mg/dL. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Assess for infection and hyperglycemia, teach not to stop abruptly, and discuss lowest effective dose/taper only as prescribed.
items.rationale: Corticosteroids suppress immune response, raise glucose, and require tapering after prolonged use.

items.title: A client receiving gentamicin reports tinnitus and has rising creatinine. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client receiving gentamicin reports tinnitus and has rising creatinine.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Hold dose pending urgent review, notify provider, and assess renal function and drug levels as ordered.
items.rationale: Aminoglycosides can cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; early symptoms warrant prompt evaluation.

items.title: A client receiving phenytoin has nystagmus, ataxia, and slurred speech. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client receiving phenytoin has nystagmus, ataxia, and slurred speech.|response:Institute fall precautions, obtain level and medication review, and notify provider before further dosing.|rationale:Nystagmus and ataxia are common signs of elevated phenytoin levels.
items.rationale: Nystagmus and ataxia are common signs of elevated phenytoin levels.

items.title: Before metoprolol, a client's HR is 48/min and BP is 90/54 mm Hg. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Beta blocker and bradycardia|priority:Hold dose according to prescribed parameters, assess symptoms and perfusion, and notify provider.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Beta blockers reduce heart rate and blood pressure; symptomatic bradycardia/hypotension requires review.

items.title: A client taking clopidogrel reports new black stools and weakness. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Antiplatelet therapy|actions:Assess for bleeding and hemodynamic compromise, notify provider urgently, and do not advise stopping long-term therapy without prescriber direction.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Clopidogrel increases bleeding risk; suspected GI hemorrhage needs urgent assessment.

items.title: An older adult is admitted with multiple medication bottles and cannot recall doses. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:An older adult is admitted with multiple medication bottles and cannot recall doses.|priority:Obtain a best possible medication history from the client, caregiver, pharmacy, and records; reconcile discrepancies before administration.
items.rationale: Multiple sources reduce omissions, duplication, and dosing errors during transitions.

items.title: Twenty minutes after birth, a client has heavy vaginal bleeding and a boggy fundus. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Uterine atony is a common cause of postpartum hemorrhage; rapid response limits shock.

items.title: A 34-week pregnant client has BP 168/112 mm Hg, severe headache, and visual spots. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Severe-range hypertension and neurologic symptoms increase risk of stroke and eclampsia.

items.title: A pregnant client with preeclampsia begins a tonic-clonic seizure. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Protect airway and client from injury, position laterally when possible, call emergency response, and administer magnesium sulfate per protocol.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Maternal stabilization and seizure control are immediate priorities; avoid restraining the client.

items.title: A 32-week pregnant client has painless bright-red vaginal bleeding and a soft nontender uterus. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Avoid vaginal examination, assess maternal/fetal status, establish IV access, and notify obstetric team.
items.rationale: Digital examination can disrupt placenta previa and cause catastrophic hemorrhage.

items.title: A pregnant client has sudden abdominal pain, dark bleeding, uterine tenderness, and frequent contractions. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Placental abruption|actions:Escalate immediately, assess maternal circulation and fetal status, establish IV access, and prepare for urgent delivery if indicated.|evaluation:Painful bleeding and uterine tenderness suggest abruption with risk of maternal hemorrhage and fetal compromise.
items.rationale: Painful bleeding and uterine tenderness suggest abruption with risk of maternal hemorrhage and fetal compromise.

items.title: After membrane rupture, fetal heart rate falls to 70/min and the cord is visible at the introitus. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Call emergency obstetric response, use a gloved hand to lift presenting part off cord, position knee-chest/Trendelenburg, and prepare for immediate birth.
items.rationale: Relieving cord compression preserves fetal oxygenation while expediting delivery.

items.title: During oxytocin infusion, recurrent late decelerations occur with contractions. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Stop oxytocin, reposition laterally, increase IV fluids as appropriate, assess maternal BP, and notify obstetric provider.
items.rationale: Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency; reduce uterine stimulation and improve perfusion.

items.title: After delivery of the fetal head, the shoulders fail to deliver and the turtle sign appears. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Call for help and assist with McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure; never apply fundal pressure.
items.rationale: Shoulder dystocia requires maneuvers that widen pelvic outlet and release impacted shoulder; fundal pressure worsens impaction.

items.title: An infant of a diabetic mother is jittery at 1 hour of life; bedside glucose is 32 mg/dL. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:An infant of a diabetic mother is jittery at 1 hour of life; bedside glucose is 32 mg/dL.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Follow neonatal hypoglycemia protocol: feed promptly if stable and able, recheck glucose, and give dextrose gel/IV glucose as indicated.
items.rationale: Jitteriness may signal hypoglycemia; prompt treatment prevents neurologic injury.

items.title: A term newborn has grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, and central cyanosis. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A term newborn has grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, and central cyanosis.|response:Call neonatal team, maintain warmth, support airway/oxygenation, and monitor preductal saturation.|rationale:Grunting and retractions indicate respiratory distress requiring prompt stabilization.
items.rationale: Grunting and retractions indicate respiratory distress requiring prompt stabilization.

items.title: Two days after cesarean birth, a client has fever, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Postpartum endometritis|priority:Notify provider, obtain ordered cultures, administer prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics, and monitor for sepsis.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Postpartum fever with uterine tenderness and malodorous lochia suggests uterine infection.

items.title: An unsensitized Rh-negative client delivers an Rh-positive infant. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Rh incompatibility|actions:Administer Rh(D) immune globulin within the recommended postpartum window and assess need for additional dosing based on fetomaternal hemorrhage testing.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Rh immune globulin prevents maternal sensitization and future hemolytic disease.

items.title: A client at 30 weeks has regular contractions and cervical change. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client at 30 weeks has regular contractions and cervical change.|priority:Assess fetal/maternal status, notify obstetric team, administer prescribed antenatal corticosteroids and tocolytic when appropriate, and assess for contraindications.
items.rationale: Corticosteroids improve fetal lung maturity; tocolysis may allow time for treatment when safe.

items.title: A breastfeeding client has unilateral breast erythema, fever, and flu-like symptoms. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Milk removal supports recovery; untreated bacterial infection may progress to abscess.

items.title: A 4-year-old has high fever, drooling, tripod posture, and muffled voice. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Manipulating the airway can precipitate complete obstruction in suspected epiglottitis.

items.title: A 2-year-old has barking cough, inspiratory stridor at rest, and suprasternal retractions. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Keep child calm, provide prescribed corticosteroid and nebulized epinephrine for moderate/severe symptoms, and monitor after treatment.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Stridor at rest indicates significant upper-airway narrowing; nebulized epinephrine has temporary effect and requires observation.

items.title: An 8-month-old with RSV has nasal congestion, poor feeding, RR 62/min, and mild retractions. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Assess work of breathing and hydration, suction nasal secretions, provide oxygen if indicated, and support hydration.
items.rationale: Bronchiolitis treatment is primarily supportive; nasal suction can improve feeding and breathing.

items.title: A toddler has vomiting and diarrhea, dry mucosa, sunken eyes, and capillary refill 4 seconds. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Dehydration|actions:Assess severity and perfusion, begin oral rehydration if mild/moderate and able, or isotonic IV bolus for shock/severe dehydration per protocol.|evaluation:Rehydration route depends on perfusion and ability to tolerate oral fluids.
items.rationale: Rehydration route depends on perfusion and ability to tolerate oral fluids.

items.title: A child has 6 days of fever, bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash, and swollen hands. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Notify provider promptly and anticipate IV immunoglobulin and aspirin therapy with cardiac evaluation.
items.rationale: Early treatment reduces risk of coronary artery aneurysm.

items.title: A 10-month-old has episodic severe crying, draws knees to chest, vomits, and passes currant-jelly stool. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Keep NPO, establish IV access, monitor perfusion, and prepare for ultrasound and air/contrast enema reduction.
items.rationale: Intermittent pain and bloody mucus stool suggest intussusception; enema may be diagnostic and therapeutic.

items.title: A 5-week-old has projectile nonbilious vomiting, hunger after emesis, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Correct fluid and electrolyte deficits before surgical pyloromyotomy; monitor weight and urine output.
items.rationale: Persistent gastric losses cause dehydration and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; stabilize before surgery.

items.title: An infant with tetralogy of Fallot becomes cyanotic and irritable during feeding. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:An infant with tetralogy of Fallot becomes cyanotic and irritable during feeding.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Place infant in knee-chest position, provide oxygen, calm infant, and summon provider/emergency assistance.
items.rationale: Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance and can reduce right-to-left shunting.

items.title: A child with sickle cell disease has fever, chest pain, cough, and new pulmonary infiltrate. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A child with sickle cell disease has fever, chest pain, cough, and new pulmonary infiltrate.|response:Escalate urgently, provide oxygen if hypoxemic, initiate prescribed antibiotics/analgesia, encourage incentive spirometry, and prepare transfusion evaluation.|rationale:Acute chest syndrome is life-threatening and requires prompt supportive and disease-specific care.
items.rationale: Acute chest syndrome is life-threatening and requires prompt supportive and disease-specific care.

items.title: A 20-month-old has a generalized seizure lasting 2 minutes during fever and is now drowsy but breathing. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Febrile seizure|priority:Protect airway and safety, time the event, assess recovery and glucose as indicated, and educate caregiver after evaluation.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Brief generalized febrile seizures are often self-limited; airway safety and assessment for cause are essential.

items.title: A child has fever, lethargy, hypotension, and a rapidly spreading nonblanching petechial rash. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Meningococcemia|actions:Initiate droplet precautions, activate sepsis response, obtain cultures without delaying antibiotics, and support circulation.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Meningococcal sepsis can progress rapidly; isolation and immediate treatment are critical.

items.title: A 3-year-old has bruises in different healing stages and an injury explanation inconsistent with developmental ability. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A 3-year-old has bruises in different healing stages and an injury explanation inconsistent with developmental ability.|priority:Ensure immediate safety, document objective findings and exact statements, and follow mandatory reporting policy.
items.rationale: Inconsistent history and patterned injuries require safeguarding and mandated reporting, not independent investigation.

items.title: A child has periorbital edema, 4+ proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and weight gain. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Protein loss causes hypoalbuminemia and edema; infection and thrombosis risks require monitoring.

items.title: A school-age child develops cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, and hypertension 2 weeks after strep throat. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis causes inflammation, hematuria, fluid retention, and hypertension.

items.title: A child with type 1 diabetes has fever and vomiting with glucose 280 mg/dL. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Continue basal insulin as directed, check glucose and ketones frequently, encourage fluids, and seek urgent care for persistent vomiting or moderate/large ketones.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Illness increases insulin needs; stopping insulin can precipitate DKA.

items.title: A hospitalized child with autism becomes distressed by alarms and unexpected touch. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Use predictable routines, simple concrete language, sensory accommodations, caregiver input, and advance warning before procedures.
items.rationale: Individualized communication and sensory support reduce distress and improve cooperation.

items.title: A client says, “I have a plan to take all my pills tonight,” and has access to medications. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Suicide risk|actions:Maintain continuous observation, remove access to means, initiate immediate safety precautions, and notify mental health/emergency team.|evaluation:Specific plan, intent, and access indicate imminent risk requiring immediate protection.
items.rationale: Specific plan, intent, and access indicate imminent risk requiring immediate protection.

items.title: A client with bipolar disorder has slept 2 hours in 3 days, speaks rapidly, and spends impulsively. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Reduce stimulation, set clear limits, support hydration/nutrition and sleep, and administer prescribed mood-stabilizing treatment.
items.rationale: A structured low-stimulation environment reduces escalation and supports physiologic needs.

items.title: A client reports voices commanding them to harm a roommate. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Assess command content, intent, and ability to resist; protect potential targets, maintain observation, and notify team immediately.
items.rationale: Command hallucinations with potential harm require direct risk assessment and immediate safety planning.

items.title: A client experiencing sudden intense fear has palpitations, trembling, and hyperventilation; medical causes are being assessed. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Remain with client, use calm brief statements, reduce stimuli, and coach slow breathing after ensuring medical stability.
items.rationale: Presence and simple grounding reduce panic; do not dismiss symptoms before excluding medical causes.

items.title: A client beginning lithium asks how to prevent toxicity during hot weather. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client beginning lithium asks how to prevent toxicity during hot weather.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Maintain consistent fluid and sodium intake, avoid dehydration, attend serum-level/renal monitoring, and contact provider for vomiting or diarrhea.
items.rationale: Fluid and sodium depletion can raise lithium concentrations and cause toxicity.

items.title: A client taking sertraline starts linezolid and develops agitation, diaphoresis, hyperreflexia, and fever. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client taking sertraline starts linezolid and develops agitation, diaphoresis, hyperreflexia, and fever.|response:Stop serotonergic agents pending urgent review, obtain emergency assessment, and support cooling/fluids as prescribed.|rationale:Serotonin toxicity can be life-threatening; medication interaction and neuromuscular findings are key clues.
items.rationale: Serotonin toxicity can be life-threatening; medication interaction and neuromuscular findings are key clues.

items.title: A client taking haloperidol has fever 40°C, severe rigidity, confusion, and autonomic instability. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Neuroleptic malignant syndrome|priority:Stop antipsychotic, initiate emergency medical response, provide supportive cooling/hydration, and anticipate prescribed specific therapy.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: NMS is a life-threatening reaction requiring immediate discontinuation and supportive management.

items.title: A client admitted after heavy alcohol use is tremulous and has a history of withdrawal seizure. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Alcohol use disorder|actions:Use validated withdrawal scale, institute seizure precautions, administer prescribed benzodiazepine, and give thiamine before or with glucose when feasible.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Prior withdrawal seizure increases risk of complicated withdrawal; thiamine reduces Wernicke risk.

items.title: A severely malnourished client begins nutritional rehabilitation and develops weakness; phosphate falls to 1.2 mg/dL. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A severely malnourished client begins nutritional rehabilitation and develops weakness; phosphate falls to 1.2 mg/dL.|priority:Notify provider, monitor phosphate/potassium/magnesium and cardiac status, and slow/adjust feeding as prescribed.
items.rationale: Refeeding syndrome causes dangerous intracellular electrolyte shifts, especially hypophosphatemia.

items.title: An older adult with stable dementia becomes acutely inattentive and disoriented over 12 hours. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Acute fluctuating change is delirium until evaluated, not expected dementia progression.

items.title: A client says, “My diagnosis means my life is over.” The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Open-ended reflection encourages expression and assessment of the client's concerns.

items.title: A client with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is admitted with cough, night sweats, and weight loss. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Place in airborne infection isolation, use fit-tested respirator, and obtain sputum specimens as ordered.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Pulmonary TB spreads via airborne particles and requires airborne precautions.

items.title: A nurse sustains a hollow-bore needlestick after blood exposure. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Wash area, report immediately, document exposure, and obtain urgent occupational-health assessment for HIV/HBV/HCV postexposure management.
items.rationale: Time-sensitive risk assessment and prophylaxis reduce transmission risk.

items.title: An outdoor worker is confused with core temperature 40.5°C and hot skin. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Heat stroke|actions:Activate emergency response and begin rapid active cooling while supporting airway/circulation; do not delay cooling for antipyretics.|evaluation:Heat stroke is thermoregulatory failure; rapid cooling is lifesaving and antipyretics are ineffective.
items.rationale: Heat stroke is thermoregulatory failure; rapid cooling is lifesaving and antipyretics are ineffective.

items.title: Several household members have headache and nausea after a faulty heater; pulse oximetry reads 99%. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Remove from exposure, administer high-concentration oxygen, obtain carboxyhemoglobin testing, and evaluate for hyperbaric therapy when indicated.
items.rationale: Standard pulse oximetry may appear normal because it cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin.

items.title: A client with hypertension and atrial fibrillation asks how to reduce stroke risk. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Reinforce BP control, prescribed anticoagulation adherence, smoking cessation, and urgent response to FAST symptoms.
items.rationale: Atrial fibrillation and hypertension are modifiable stroke risks; anticoagulation reduces embolic stroke risk when indicated.

items.title: A severely immunocompromised client asks about receiving a live attenuated vaccine. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Verify immune status and vaccine-specific guidance; defer live vaccine when contraindicated and consult immunization provider.
items.rationale: Live vaccines may cause disease in severe immunosuppression; decisions depend on the specific condition and vaccine.

items.title: After a mass-casualty event, a walking client has minor abrasions while another is apneic. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:After a mass-casualty event, a walking client has minor abrasions while another is apneic.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Use the established triage system and reassess; direct walking wounded to designated area while evaluating the apneic client per protocol.
items.rationale: Disaster triage prioritizes greatest survivable benefit with limited resources; follow local START/JumpSTART protocol.

items.title: An immobile older adult has intact skin with nonblanchable erythema over the sacrum. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:An immobile older adult has intact skin with nonblanchable erythema over the sacrum.|response:Offload pressure, reposition based on individualized plan, manage moisture, support nutrition, and document skin findings.|rationale:Nonblanchable erythema indicates a stage 1 pressure injury; pressure relief prevents progression.
items.rationale: Nonblanchable erythema indicates a stage 1 pressure injury; pressure relief prevents progression.

items.title: An older adult with orthostatic hypotension fell while walking to the bathroom at night. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Fall prevention|priority:Assess injury and orthostatic vitals, review medications, provide assisted toileting and environmental modifications, and use individualized fall precautions.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Addressing orthostasis and environmental hazards reduces recurrent falls.

items.title: A new ileostomy appears dusky purple and has stopped producing output with increasing abdominal pain. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Ostomy assessment|actions:Notify surgeon urgently and assess perfusion/obstruction; a healthy stoma should be moist and pink to red.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Dusky discoloration suggests ischemia; absent output with pain may indicate obstruction.

items.title: A client with an AV fistula has no palpable thrill or audible bruit. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client with an AV fistula has no palpable thrill or audible bruit.|priority:Do not use the access; notify dialysis team immediately and assess distal circulation.
items.rationale: Absent thrill/bruit suggests thrombosis or access failure requiring urgent evaluation.

items.title: A client on peritoneal dialysis reports abdominal pain and cloudy effluent. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Cloudy effluent and abdominal pain are classic signs of peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis.
